vignette:
He is sixty-seven now, a physician who has spent most of his adult life moving steadily through crisis with a practiced calm. In the hospital, colleagues know him as measured and precise, a man who can deliver bad news gently and keep his hands steady during emergencies. He lives alone, has been single for many years, and keeps a disciplined routine that once gave him a sense of order. When he speaks about what happened to his son, though, that professional composure begins to fray. He tells the story carefully at first, like a doctor presenting a case, but it soon becomes clear that he is still living inside it.

His son was in his thirties when he became critically ill. What began as a vague complaint turned, over a frighteningly short period of time, into a life-threatening medical crisis. As a doctor, he understood the significance of each lab value, each delayed response, each subtle change in appearance before anyone had to say it aloud. He remembers the fluorescent lights in the ICU, the rhythm of monitors, the particular smell of antiseptic and stale coffee in family waiting rooms. He remembers standing at the bedside while trying to occupy two impossible roles at once: physician and father. He could interpret the treatment plan, challenge decisions, anticipate complications. None of that protected him from the terror of watching his child struggle to stay alive.

During those days and nights, he barely slept. He remained alert to every alarm, every footstep in the hallway. If a nurse took too long to answer a call light, his chest tightened and his mind leapt immediately to catastrophe. He found himself staring at the monitor as if vigilance alone could keep his son alive. When he did close his eyes, he saw his son's face as it looked during the worst moments-drained, frightened, dependent on machines and on other people's judgment. He still feels ashamed of how often he mentally rehearsed the possibility of his son dying, as if preparing himself could somehow blunt the blow.

His son survived, but he says that survival did not bring the relief he had imagined. Instead, after the crisis passed, his body seemed unable to stand down. He returned to work and expected himself to function normally. Outwardly, he did. He saw patients, wrote notes, made rounds. Internally, he was pulled back again and again to the ICU. Certain sounds-a monitor beeping, the hiss of oxygen, even the squeak of rubber-soled shoes on hospital floors-send a shock through him before he can think. He becomes briefly disoriented, his heart pounding, as if some part of him is back beside that bed waiting for bad news.

He notices that he avoids parts of the hospital that remind him too clearly of that period. Although critical care used to feel familiar, he now finds reasons to delegate tasks that take him near the ICU. If he cannot avoid it, he braces himself before entering, jaw tight, eyes scanning. He does not speak much about his son's illness with family or colleagues. In his cultural world, he says, fathers are expected to be strong, and doctors even more so. He has spent a lifetime being the person others lean on. He cannot bear the feeling of losing control, so he keeps the worst of it to himself.

At home, the nights are hardest. He sleeps lightly and wakes suddenly, sometimes with the image of his son dying before he reaches the bed. On those nights he gets up and checks his phone to make sure there is no missed call, no message, no new emergency. He knows his son is no longer in immediate danger, yet he remains on guard, as though disaster has merely paused. If his son does not respond to a text quickly, he feels irritation first and then fear. He calls, then tries to sound casual when his son answers. Afterward, he is embarrassed by the intensity of his reaction, but not reassured.

He has become more withdrawn over time. Friends have noticed that he declines invitations and leaves gatherings early. He says he is tired, but what he means is that ordinary conversation feels flimsy against the constant pressure inside him. He is more easily angered now, especially when people seem careless or dismissive about illness. At work, he can become sharply critical with trainees when they miss details, and afterward he recognizes that his reactions are stronger than the situation warrants. He tells himself that vigilance saves lives, yet he also knows he is no longer responding only to the present moment.

What troubles him most is the change in how he sees the world. Before his son's illness, medicine had taught him that outcomes could be uncertain, but he still believed competence and devotion offered some protection. Now he feels exposed to how quickly life can turn. He says he no longer experiences safety as a real condition, only as a temporary illusion. Even when he sits quietly in his apartment after a long day, there is a part of him listening for the next alarm.
